text: Good morning, Your Honor. My name is Emily Smart Warner. I'm appearing on behalf of the city of Cincinnati. And I'm ready to proceed.

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: Good morning, Your Honor, and may it please the court. My name is Emily Smart Warner, and I represent the appellant, City of Cincinnati. In this case, the trial court erred in three ways. First, the trial court erred in granting judgment to the gun advocate groups by deciding that the city's ordinance conflicted with revised code 9.68. Second, the trial court erred in finding that the Buckeye Firearms Foundation has standing. And third, the trial court abused its discretion in awarding nearly $170,000 in fees and costs to the attorneys and the plaintiffs in this case. So first, I'd like to address the conflict issue, the statutory interpretation issue. What the city of Cincinnati did in the wake of the tragic Las Vegas shooting that seems so distant today, but is still very important, was it took a step to ban the possession of trigger activators within the city of Cincinnati. Now, these are devices that are generally attached to firearms, often semi-automatic firearms. And their sole purpose is to have those firearms approximate the speed of automatic fire. So that's part of the reason why the Las Vegas shooting was so deadly. That is the devices that the city of Cincinnati banned. Now importantly, this ordinance that banned the possession of trigger activators did not conflict with the state law, revised code 9.68, that preempts many of the city's ability to regulate the possession of firearms.

speaker: bethmyers
text: And can you tell us why you think it does not conflict?

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: Yes, Your Honor. It does not conflict because revised code 9.68 regulates, it preempts cities on the possession of firearms, parts, and components. It is silent on the regulation of accessories. And these trigger activators are accessories to firearms, not parts or components of firearms. This court's review of this issue is de novo. So what the court must do is look at what the city's ordinance bans, what revised code 9.68 preempts, and it must find a conflict between the two. Importantly, there is no preemption by occupation of the fields for this kind of home rule analysis. Now the city agrees that the ordinance was a police power. So if there is a conflict, we would be preempted. But the record before the court demonstrates that these devices are accessories. When you're trying to figure out what's an accessory and what's a part or a component, the court engages in a familiar statutory interpretation process. You look at the words. Now 9.68 doesn't define parts or components. Accessory isn't defined here. So what you would look at is the dictionary definitions of the words, how they are used in their plain and ordinary usage. And what the city provided you in its briefing is that accessories are things that are of secondary importance. They are usually mountable or demountable. They add to the convenience of the device. Whereas a part is constituent, it is a component without which the article could not function.

speaker: candacecrouse
text: Aren't several of these trigger mechanisms pieces that have to be mounted and permanently installed on a firearm? And I mean, isn't that like what a bump stock is and what several of these items are? You have to actually, you replace a part that's already on the firearm and you install it and attach it to the firearm?

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: Sometimes yes and sometimes no. So for a bump stock, what the bump stock does, it is a replacement for the typical standard stock. And it alters how you fire the rifle. So instead of pulling the trigger, you're actually pulling the firearm forward so that the recoil causes the firearm to move in the bump stock. But you add that on, you can take it off. It's a relatively simple process. But for some of the other trigger activators, the record demonstrates that, for example, like a trigger crank. So this is just, it can slide in with a couple of screws near the trigger part. And then there's a crank that you turn instead of firing the trigger. That you can take off on and off within a matter of minutes. Which demonstrates that these are more accessories to the firearms. They are not the trigger for the firearm.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: Let me ask you, ma'am. It sounds like under your definition of a component, it must be an original part. That's part of the firearm when it's purchased. Is that fair to say?

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: Your honor, typically. So there's always going to be exceptions to these rules. And I think that that's something that the city's expert recognized. So I think there are many manufacturers who are going to custom build firearms. So there was one manufacturer that will sell you a firearm with a binary trigger. But when the court is applying the definition and trying to distinguish between accessories and component parts. I think you look at the ordinary course. And in the area of for these excise taxes, federal excise tax. That's what the Code of Federal Regulations does. Is it looks, is it ordinarily part of your standard issue? And so in part, yes, your honor. I think it is indicative of whether it's an accessory or component of whether it is part of your standard stock that you're going to get from the manufacturer, but there could be exceptions to these rules. So you need to look at what is ordinarily going to occur.

speaker: candacecrouse
text: What do you do in the situation of somebody who wants to put together their own firearm and then they wanna buy a bunch of parts and put it together, right? So then it becomes kind of, it's originally put together with maybe one of these trigger activators. Would it be an accessory at that point? Or does it become a component then?

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: I think, again, you have to look at, is it typically used that way? So you can customize a variety of things, but is a bump stock ordinarily going to be the stock for a rifle? No, none of the experts testified to that.

speaker: candacecrouse
text: Not something that you could purchase from a manufacturer. But I'm just saying that if you wanna just put your own rifle together and that the bump stock is the stock that you pick, and then you put it together. Is it still an accessory or is it a component at that point because it was built that way?

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: Your honor, we would argue that it still remains an accessory to the firearm. Because just because one person decides that they want to put together a firearm from scratch using these different parts, it doesn't change that these are ordinarily going to be parts that you don't get from the manufacturer, that you're adding on after purchase, that you're taking on and off when you want to get closer to automatic fire.

speaker: bethmyers
text: The statute, in effect at the time, didn't make this distinction between component and accessory, did it?

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: The statute was silent on accessory, and after it was extensively amended by the General Assembly, it still remained silent on accessory. So accessory has never been a part of 9.68.

speaker: bethmyers
text: And you're reading it into the statute, then. The distinction you're making is not a statutory distinction.

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: It is, your honor, in the fact that the General Assembly decided not to include accessories to firearms in the preemption, and there has to be a specific conflict for the city's home rule authority to be preempted. So the statute, as the General Assembly drafted it, is silent as to accessories. They were amending it while these lawsuits were being litigated in Cincinnati and Columbus. They still chose not to add the word accessory to the statute. So unless and until they specifically preempt cities from regulating firearms accessories, they have not, there is no conflict.

speaker: candacecrouse
text: Didn't your expert actually testify, I'm trying to remember this because I did read his deposition, that if you build a gun, for example, with a bump stock. And somebody, I guess that's called gunsmithing, and it's put together with the bump stock, that that bump stock is then a component and not an accessory? Or am I wrong on his testimony?

speaker: emilysmartwo
text: He was, so what he was testifying to are how these devices are used in the field. And so he admitted that perhaps something that is built from scratch, that that bump stock could be considered a component of the firearm. But I think to take a step back, that expert cannot create the definition for the trier of fact. It's a legal issue for the court to decide what the meaning of these words are. So the expert testimony was helpful to the trier of fact in determining what these devices are, how they function, how they're referred to in the industry. But they cannot create the legal definition for this court. That's for the trier of fact to do.

speaker: bethmyers
